cards.explanation: The answer is on their hearts and their altars. The LORD says the sin is engraved "…on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars." So it's carved into the inside of the people and into the place where they worshiped (Jeremiah 17:1). A diamond point isn't something you wipe off with a damp rag, friends.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "Even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills." So the text says they remember, not that they've forgotten (Jeremiah 17:2). The children aren't forgetting a thing, and I think that's what makes this verse so heavy.

The answer is to give them over as plunder. The LORD says, "…I will give over your wealth and all your treasures as plunder, because of the sin of your high places…" (Jeremiah 17:3). Plunder is what enemies carry off, friends. The treasures aren't staying put.

The answer is in a land they do not know. The LORD says, "I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know…" (Jeremiah 17:4). It's not just that they lose the inheritance. They end up somewhere unfamiliar. I think that's a hard thing to hear.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "…you have kindled My anger; it will burn forever" (Jeremiah 17:4). There's no burning out soon in these words. This is a heavy part of the passage, friends, and it's good to take it seriously.

The answer is a shrub in the desert. The LORD says the man who trusts in mankind "…will be like a shrub in the desert…" (Jeremiah 17:5-6). A shrub out in the desert, bakers. Hardly a picture of someone who's doing well.
The answer is True. The LORD says of this man, "he will not see when prosperity comes" (Jeremiah 17:6). Good things can come, and he still doesn't see them. That's a hard way to live, friends.

The answer is waters. The man who trusts in the LORD is "…like a tree planted by the waters…" (Jeremiah 17:8). Compare that to the shrub in the desert, bakers. This tree is planted right where the water is.

The answer is its roots. This tree "…sends out its roots toward the stream" (Jeremiah 17:8). The roots are doing the reaching, friends, and that's where the tree gets its water. Slow work, but it's steady.

The answer is False. The LORD says the tree "…does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit" (Jeremiah 17:8). Even in a dry year, the fruit keeps coming. Roots by the stream, remember, bakers.

The answer is the LORD Himself. The question was who can understand the deceitful heart (Jeremiah 17:9), and here's the answer. The LORD says, "I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind…" (Jeremiah 17:10). He can, friends.

The answer is deeds. The LORD says He searches the heart "…to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve" (Jeremiah 17:10). It's about the way a man lives and what he does, bakers. That's the word.

The answer is a man who makes a fortune unjustly. The LORD says, "Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly" (Jeremiah 17:11). A partridge sitting on eggs she did not lay, friends. That's the picture of a fortune made unjustly.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "In the middle of his days his riches will desert him, and in the end he will be the fool" (Jeremiah 17:11). The riches don't stay all his days, bakers. They leave him partway through.

The answer is the fountain of living water. The prayer says they "…have abandoned the LORD, the fountain of living water" (Jeremiah 17:13). Think about what that means, friends. They walked away from the very source of water, and I think that's a heavy picture.

The answer is that it come now. The people say, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!" (Jeremiah 17:15). They want it to show up right then, bakers. And the one praying says they keep saying it to him.
The answer is True. The one praying says, "I have not desired the day of despair" (Jeremiah 17:16). He's telling the LORD he didn't want it, friends. And he adds that the LORD knows what he said.
The answer is True. The one praying says, "You are my refuge in the day of disaster" (Jeremiah 17:17). It's a short line, bakers, but it says a lot about where he runs when things go bad.

The answer is shame for them but not for him. The prayer says, "Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame" (Jeremiah 17:18). It's the cry of someone being persecuted, friends. I think it's a hard prayer, and the text just lets it stand.
